tagline.text: A day hike along the Iriga crater ridge overlooking Lake Buhi

location.label: Location
location.text: Iriga City and Buhi, Camarines Sur (Mount Iriga)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500–1,500 (transport, guide and meals; confirm guide rates locally)

children.text: Mount Asog (Mount Iriga) is a dormant volcano straddling Iriga City and Buhi in Camarines Sur, known for its horseshoe-shaped crater at about 1,140–1,196 m and for views of Lake Buhi and Mayon Volcano. The Ilian route allows a day hike, and it is safest to climb with a guide.

Mount Asog, also called Mount Iriga, is an andesitic stratovolcano straddling Iriga City and Buhi in Camarines Sur. Wikipedia gives its height as 1,196 m, while hiking guides such as Pinoy Mountaineer list about 1,140 m. Its base is about
10km
across, and it stands about
1km
from Lake Buhi. It lies between Mount Isarog to the north and Mayon Volcano to the south, and some people combine it with an Isarog climb.

The mountain's defining feature is its horseshoe-shaped crater, where one side has collapsed. Wikipedia says the volcano is known for phreatic explosions, that it erupted in 1628 and 1642, and that a flank failure on the southeast side formed a large crater. The resulting debris avalanche is said to have buried villages about
4km

from the summit. The Iriga City article on Wikipedia describes an eruption on January 4, 1641 and a gully formed on the Buhi side, so the dates differ by source; just remember it as a 17th-century event. The volcano is now classified as dormant, and the mountain has several springs that supply clean water to the town and neighboring towns.
Two hiking routes are known. The easiest and most widely used route is the Ilian route in the village of San Nicolas, Iriga City, and one guide says it can be done as a day hike with about
4 hours

to the summit. The quieter route starts from Cabatuan in Buhi, passes the Esplana campsite and goes up to the dead crater, and usually takes two days and one night. The mountain is rated 4 out of 9 in difficulty and classified as a minor climb. A solo hiker's review gives about
5.6km
from Ilian to the summit with an elevation gain of about

and calls it a cardiac trail of constant uphill. Some sections are said to be 45–60 degrees steep. That review reports no leeches, but other guides mention leeches and rattan vines, so long pants are the safe choice.

From the summit you can see the crater and ridges, Lake Buhi and Lake Bato, Mount Isarog, Mount Malinao, Mount Masaraga, Mayon Volcano and, to the east, Catanduanes Island. However, clouds are frequent, and one reviewer says the lake and villages appeared only when the clouds parted. Most of the route is exposed to the sun, so it is very hot at midday. Start early with a guide, and confirm fees and registration locally.
The crater, open on one side because of the collapsed slope, is the identity of this mountain. From the ridge you can see steep, narrow grassy ridges running down toward the crater.

When the clouds lift, you can see Lake Buhi and nearby towns far below. From below, this is the mountain that stands behind the lake. One reviewer describes an unobstructed 360-degree view from the summit of the broken caldera, Mount Isarog, Mount Malinao, Lake Bato, Lake Buhi and Mayon Volcano.

Sources say that from the summit you can see the cone of Mayon Volcano and Mount Malinao and Mount Masaraga to the south, and Mount Isarog to the north. Catanduanes Island is said to be visible to the east.
This is the easiest route, starting from Ilian in San Nicolas. One guide says you reach the summit in about
4 hours
. You pass coconut plantations and grazing grassland before entering forest. A 2011 review describes passing Inagta villages at the start, then woodland and grassland before reaching the crater rim.
One itinerary describes resting at Kubo-Kubo, at about 685 m, after about an hour and a half. The trail gets steeper past this point.

blocks.title: The Esplana route and the dead crater

children.text: This quieter route starts from Cabatuan in Buhi. Using the Esplana campsite as a base, you climb to the dead crater and the summit, and a two-day trip is typical.
Most of the mountain is exposed to the sun, and grassy ridges continue. The scenery of wind passing over the grassland is charming, but it is very hot at midday.
One guide describes Asog as an easy day hike that is often paired with Mount Isarog in Naga City.

items.title: Ilian day hike
items.subtitle: Out of Iriga and back from the summit

children.text: Arrive in Naga City. If you took an overnight bus from Manila, you get off in the early morning.
Across from the Naga central bus terminal, take a van or jeepney to Iriga City and get off at the San Nicolas barangay hall.
Take a tricycle to Ilian, register and hire a guide.
Start hiking. You pass coconut plantations and grassland.
Rest at Kubo-Kubo, at about 685 m.
Reach the summit (about 1,140 m). Enjoy views of the crater, lakes and volcanoes, and have lunch.
Start the descent.
Return to Ilian and take a tricycle to Iriga City.
This schedule is an example from one hiking guide. The mobile signal is said to be good all along the route, but the weather near the summit can change quickly, so allow extra time.

items.title: Esplana route, 2 days and 1 night
items.subtitle: Out of Buhi, with a visit to the dead crater

children.text: Take a jeepney from Iriga to Buhi, register and start from the village of Cabatuan.
Arrive at Esplana Base Camp, have lunch and rest.
In the afternoon, look around the dead crater. An older guide says this takes about
2.5 hours
On the second day, start the summit climb. One guide says you reach the summit in about
3 hours
Descend to the base camp and then down to Santiago village on the Iriga side.
This itinerary is based on an old guide written in 2007 and updated in 2015. Confirm the current trail and guide situation locally.
A bus from Manila to Naga takes about
9–11 hours
, according to one guide. Iriga lies between Naga and Legazpi.
At the Naga central bus terminal, take a van or jeepney to Iriga. In Iriga, get off in front of the San Nicolas barangay hall and take a tricycle to Ilian.
You can use Naga Airport (WNP) or Bicol International Airport (DRP), but routes and schedules change often. Check the latest information.
From the airport to Iriga you must travel overland, and the time depends on traffic.
To go via Buhi, take a jeepney from Iriga to Buhi town, then register and start from the village of Cabatuan.
One guide says vans run from Naga to Buhi if you want to see the lake and Buhi town together.
The Ilian registration point is described as the site of the old CAFGU detachment, but facilities may have changed. Ask locally how to find a guide.
For the descent, you can return the same way or go down to Santiago village on the Iriga side or San Roque village on the Buhi side, according to one guide.
Most of the mountain is exposed to the sun, so hot daytime hours are hard. The cooler period is December to February, and it is best to start early and reach the summit before lunch.

In the rainy season the path is slippery and views can be hidden by cloud. The mountain is known for frequent cloud and fog, so check the weather. One guide says there is no water along the route, so carry plenty even in the dry season.

It is convenient to stay in Iriga City before and after the climb. One guide lists Iriga Plaza Hotel, Max n' Fe Apartelle, Asog County Hotel and Parkview Hotel. Staying in Naga City and traveling in the morning is also common. Room rates vary by date, so check a booking site.

Food in Iriga City and the Bicol region is often cooked with coconut milk and red chili peppers. There is reportedly no water on the mountain, so carry packed meals and plenty of water. After the climb, rest and enjoy Bicolano food in Iriga town. Iriga's feast day is
June 13
for Saint Anthony of Padua, and a harvest festival called Tinagba is also held. Lodging gets crowded during festivals, so book early.

The local language is Rinconada Bikol, and Filipino and English are also widely understood. Place names may be spelled differently on different maps, so check them against a map app. Before you set out, agree on the route and the expected time with your guide.
Start early. The upper sections are fully exposed to the sun and very hot at midday.
One guide says there is no water along the route, so carry at least 2 liters.
Bring a long-sleeve top, a hat and sunscreen. One reader recommended a long-sleeve top.
You hire a guide at Ilian. Rates depend on group size and season, so ask first.
Reviews mention leeches and rattan thorns. Long pants and gloves help.
One guide says the summit campsite fits only about two tents, so group camping is difficult.
One review says the mobile signal is strong, but download your map app for offline use anyway.
Combining the climb with Mount Isarog or Lake Buhi makes a fuller trip.
Near the summit there are knife-edged slopes and grass-covered rock faces. If clouds or fog roll in suddenly, it is easy to lose the way, so always climb with a guide.
With no water and sun-exposed trail, watch out for dehydration and heatstroke.
A review says some sections are 45–60 degrees steep, which is hard on the knees and stamina.
Descending grassy, overgrown slopes can be slippery.
Registration, guides and fees differ between guides, so be sure to confirm them locally.
The grassy ridge along the crater rim is steep at its edges. Do not stand too close to the edge when taking photos.
A lake at the foot of the mountain, home to the sinarapan, known as the world's smallest commercially harvested fish. It can also be seen from the summit.
A stratovolcano that rises behind Naga City and is climbed in the same region.
The cone-shaped volcano visible to the south from the summit.
The main city to the north of Iriga, a base for transport and lodging.
The main city of Albay, continuing south from Iriga.
